_note: DEMO DATA — every item, number, company and publication in this file is invented so the app can be evaluated without real inbox content.

main.headline: Central banks stop agreeing: the first split decision season in three years
main.one_liner: Two (fictional) major central banks cut, one holds, one hikes — the synchronized cycle is over.
bullets: The divergence is deliberate: domestic services inflation, not global goods prices, now drives each decision.
FX desks expect carry trades to return as rate differentials widen for the first time since the tightening cycle.
The odd one out — the hiker — is fighting a housing rebound, not consumer prices.
main.so_what: Divergent policy means currency volatility is back as an asset class — hedging costs stop being a rounding error for importers.

main.headline: The dividend comeback nobody priced
main.one_liner: Payout ratios are rising off a decade low — and the market is still valuing growers like hoarders.
bullets: Aggregate payout ratio up 3 points from the trough (invented figure); buyback share of returns down for a second year.
Screen of the week: firms growing dividends off low bases with net cash — 27 names, mostly industrials.
The behavioural angle: dividend growth is the easiest signal for retail investors to actually hold through drawdowns.

main.headline: Agents meet the org chart
main.one_liner: The (fictional) enterprises getting value from agentic AI all did the same unglamorous thing first: wrote down their processes.
bullets: Pattern across 12 invented case studies: agent projects succeed where the workflow was already documented, fail where it lived in heads.
The winning deployment shape: narrow agent, wide logging, human approval at the irreversible steps.
Procurement teams have started asking for audit trails of agent decisions — governance is becoming a feature.
main.so_what: Agentic AI is a process-documentation forcing function — the transformation cost was always the org, not the model.

main.headline: GCC hiring shifts from headcount to seniority
main.one_liner: Global capability centers keep growing, but the growth moved up the pyramid.
bullets: Fresh (invented) survey: GCC net additions flat year-on-year, while architect-and-above roles grew 19%.
The new mandate: product ownership and platform engineering, not seat-count arbitrage.
Tier-2 city expansion continues for cost reasons — but the senior roles cluster stubbornly in the metros.

main.headline: The paperwork moat: why compliance software keeps compounding
main.one_liner: Every new filing requirement is a tailwind for the vendors — a short structural note.
bullets: Regulatory change count in our (fictional) tracker: up every year for nine years; each change is a forced software upgrade.
Switching costs compound: five years of filings in one vendor's format is a moat no feature list beats.
The investor takeaway: boring, mandatory, recurring — the best kind of demand.

main.headline: Rumor mill: dispatch-software firm Meridian Grid said to be raising big
main.one_liner: Term-sheet chatter puts the (fictional) battery-software firm's round at a software multiple — hardware investors are grumbling.
bullets: Two funds we spoke to (in this invented scenario) passed on valuation; both conceded the dispatch-data moat argument.
If it closes at the rumored multiple, every storage-adjacent software team's next round just got repriced.
Watch for the announcement within the week.

main.headline: On the uselessness of most market commentary
main.one_liner: An essay arguing the daily narrative industry exists to explain variance, not to predict it — and why that's fine.
bullets: The test the essay proposes: would this explanation have been written if the market had moved the other way? Usually yes.
Commentary's real product is comfort — a story that makes variance bearable enough to stay invested.
The actionable bit: consume commentary for context, never for timing.

main.headline: Late note: the inference-cost floor keeps falling
main.one_liner: Another quarter, another step down in cost per million tokens — the (invented) trendline says 10x cheaper every 18 months.
bullets: The floor price for commodity-tier inference fell ~35% this quarter across the providers we track (invented figures).
Cheap inference changes product math: features that were demos at last year's prices are margins-positive now.
The strategic question moves up the stack: if tokens are nearly free, what's scarce? Distribution and data.

curious.headline: The last lighthouse keepers
curious.one_liner: A meditation on automation's long tail — the jobs that persist decades after the technology that replaced them.
bullets: Automated lights made keepers obsolete on paper in the 1980s; a handful of stations (in this fictional telling) still staff humans for redundancy.
The pattern generalizes: the last 2% of a job resists automation for longer than the first 98% took.
Beautifully reported, gently argued — the rare automation essay with no hot take.
curious.so_what: The 'last 2% problem' is the most transferable idea in the piece — it's where the cost curves of automation always flatten.

curious.headline: The apprenticeship gap
curious.one_liner: Remote work quietly broke the way juniors used to learn — and the fixes so far are scaffolding, not solutions.
bullets: The lost channel: ambient learning — overhearing how seniors handle ambiguity — doesn't survive scheduled video calls.
Best current fixes in the (invented) firms profiled: recorded decision walkthroughs and deliberate 'watch me work' hours.
The uncomfortable conclusion: mentorship now has to be designed, because it no longer happens by osmosis.

curious.headline: Marathon training in a heatwave: the science of adapting your block
curious.one_liner: Heat is a training stimulus and an injury risk at once — the difference is dosage.
bullets: Heat adaptation shows up in 10–14 days of graded exposure; the mistake is chasing pace instead of effort in week one.
The checklist: effort-based sessions, pre-cooling for quality days, and moving long runs to dawn.
A good reminder that the watch's pace field is the least useful number in summer.

curious.headline: Why every city's food district is disappearing into the same five cuisines
curious.one_liner: A grumpy, loving essay on culinary homogenization and the economics of rent.
bullets: The argument: high rents select for cuisines with proven delivery economics, compressing variety everywhere the same way.
The counterforce is suburban strip malls — lower rent keeps the long tail of regional cooking alive.
Read it for the closing tour of a (fictional) night market that refuses to optimize.
